options.text: All finite strings over the alphabet {0, 1}
options.explanation: Countable. List them by length, then alphabetically: the empty string, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, … Every string appears at some finite position.
Countable. Each program is a finite string over a finite character set, and a subset of a countable set is countable.
Correct. These are infinite binary sequences, and Cantor's diagonal argument shows no list can contain them all.
Countable, surprisingly. Fractions can be listed by walking the grid of (numerator, denominator) pairs diagonally, skipping duplicates such as 2/4.

workedExample:
A set is countable if you can list it as a sequence that reaches every element after finitely many steps.

1. Finite strings: list by length. Countable.
2. Programs are finite strings, so a subset of (1). Countable.
3. Fractions: zig-zag through the grid of (numerator, denominator) pairs. Countable.
4. Functions from ℕ to {0, 1} are infinite bit sequences. Assume a complete list of them and build a new sequence d from the diagonal:

```formula
d(i) = 1 − s_i(i)
where
s_i: the i-th sequence in the supposed list
s_i(i): bit number i of sequence s_i (the diagonal)
d: the new sequence
d(i): bit number i of d
i: a position, 1, 2, 3, …
ℕ: the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …
In words: each bit of d is the flipped diagonal bit, so d differs from the i-th sequence at position i.
```

```
s1 = 0 1 1 0 ...
s2 = 1 0 0 1 ...
s3 = 1 1 1 0 ...
d  = 1 1 0 ...
```

d differs from every listed sequence somewhere, so it is missing from the list. Uncountable.

Combining (2) and (4): there are more yes/no problems than programs, so some problems cannot be solved by any program.
